what: Cavco Industries builds factory-made homes. It manufactures manufactured and modular houses in plants and ships them to sites, sells them through its own retail stores and independent dealers, and runs a finance arm that lends to buyers and an insurance business.
customers: Buyers of affordable homes, particularly in the southern and western United States, plus community owners and developers buying homes in volume.
money: Manufactured and modular homes built in plants and sold through retail and dealers.
Mortgage lending to buyers of its homes, and insurance.
moat: Building a house in a factory costs substantially less per square foot than building it on site, because the labour is in one place, the weather is irrelevant and materials are bought in volume. That cost advantage matters most where housing is least affordable, which is increasingly everywhere. Owning the retail stores and the lending arm captures margin along the whole chain.
risks: The shares trade at about 27.5 times earnings and 18.5 times EV/EBITDA, which is a full price for a housing manufacturer.
Revenue swung from $2.1B in 2023 to $1.8B in 2024, showing how quickly demand moves with interest rates.
Buyers of these homes are more sensitive to interest rates and credit availability than conventional homebuyers.
Only five analysts cover the stock, so the $725.60 average target rests on thin coverage.
The lending arm means Cavco carries credit risk on its own customers, which concentrates the exposure.
opportunities: Debt of only $35.4M against $253.0M of cash is a remarkably clean balance sheet for a housing company.
Revenue has recovered to $2.2B in 2026, with trailing revenue of $2.4B.
Factory-built homes cost substantially less per square foot, which is the right product for an affordability crisis.
Free cash flow of $232.6M on $2.4B of revenue converts well.
Owning retail stores and the lending arm captures margin that a pure manufacturer pays away.
watch: Home shipments and the average selling price. Volume is the cycle; price per home tells you about mix and pricing power.
view: Factory-built housing is the right answer to a real problem, and the economics are straightforward: building a house in a controlled factory with labour in one place and no weather delays costs materially less per square foot than building it on a site. In a country with a housing affordability crisis and a shortage of skilled construction labour, that cost advantage should be worth more over time, not less.

Cavco captures margin along the whole chain, which is the right structure for this industry. It manufactures the homes, sells many of them through its own retail stores, and lends to the buyers through its own finance arm. Each step adds margin that a pure manufacturer hands to somebody else. The lending arm also means Cavco carries credit risk on its own customers, which concentrates exposure to exactly the buyers most affected by rising rates — a genuine double exposure worth noting.

The balance sheet is exceptional for a housing business: $35 million of debt against $253 million of cash. Housing manufacturers die in downturns because they carry inventory and debt into a collapse in demand, and Cavco simply cannot. That makes the cyclicality survivable rather than existential, and it is the single best thing about the position.

The cyclicality is real though. Revenue went from $2.1 billion to $1.8 billion and back to $2.4 billion, because buyers of affordable homes are more sensitive to interest rates and credit availability than conventional buyers — a small change in monthly payment changes whether they can buy at all. At 27.5 times earnings and 18.5 times EV/EBITDA, the price assumes the recovery continues. The business deserves respect; the multiple assumes a lot. Shipments and average selling price are the two numbers.
bull: Factory-built homes keep gaining as affordability worsens, vertical integration captures margin at every step, and a debt-free balance sheet funds growth through cycles.
bear: Rates stay high and affordable-home buyers cannot qualify, shipments fall, and a 27 times earnings multiple on a cyclical manufacturer derates.
